voice.reference_text: 大家好，欢迎来到 AI 高频词。每一期，我们只讲清楚一个词：它解决什么问题，怎么理解它，以及它在现实里意味着什么。

items.text: Remember our two-knob taxi-fare machine? It learned how fares change with distance just fine.
But fares also depend on the time of day: rush hour costs more, and late night a little more too.
It can't learn that, because all it can draw is a straight line.
So how does a machine learn a pattern that bends? With a neural network.
Last time, turning the knobs was like walking downhill blindfolded, always stepping where the score drops fastest.
Today we'll build a tiny network that learns the bend, see why more layers help, and meet AlexNet.
Here's some made-up data: the same five-kilometer ride, forty-eight times, at different hours of the day.
Daytime rides cost about twenty-three dollars, just what our two-knob machine charges.
Around eight a.m. and six p.m. it spikes, and late at night it's a bit pricier.
Same two knobs, one for height and one for slope, but now we feed it the time, not the distance.
However you turn them, the best you get is a nearly flat line through the middle.
It undercharges at rush hour and overcharges by day. Its loss, the score for how wrong it is, can't get below eleven point five.
The knobs aren't the problem: this machine only draws straight lines, and the pattern bends.
The fix isn't one big machine. It's lots of simple little ones.
Each unit still has two knobs and draws a line, plus one rule: anything below zero becomes zero.
Its line stays flat, then bends upward.
The two knobs set where it bends and how steep it gets.
One bend isn't enough, so add more units that bend in different spots.
Add them up, and you can build bumps, steps, almost any curve.
Our network has twelve units side by side in the first layer, and one unit in the second.
That unit scales each bent line with a knob, adds them up, then one last knob shifts the total. That's the fare.
Thirty-seven knobs in all.
Layers of little units like this are what we call a neural network.
The name comes from neurons in the brain, but don't take that too seriously.
To turn all thirty-seven, we use last episode's trick, nudging every knob whichever way drops the loss fastest.
Our curve starts as a random squiggle, and step by step it bends toward the peaks.
After ten thousand steps, the loss is down to zero point two six. The best straight line never got below eleven point five.
Rush hours and late nights, it catches them all.
And every corner on this curve is one little unit making its bend.
By the way, there's a much faster trick for finding which way to turn each knob. More on that next time.
So far, we've put units side by side, each adding one bend.
Now stack them, so each layer folds the line it gets from the layer before, like folding paper.
For example, two units per layer can fold a slanted line exactly in half.
One layer makes two straight pieces, two layers make four, and in this example each new layer doubles that.
So ten units side by side give at most eleven pieces. Stacked five deep, they can give thirty-two.
Later layers reuse what earlier ones already folded.
The deeper the stack, the more complex the shapes the same units can build.
That's the "deep" in deep learning.
In twenty twelve, three researchers at the University of Toronto trained a very deep neural network.
Their network became known as AlexNet.
It had eight layers and sixty million knobs. It learned a thousand categories from one point two million photos.
At that year's ImageNet contest, it got five guesses per picture, and only missed if all five were wrong.
The version they entered got fifteen point three percent wrong. The runner-up got twenty-six point two.
Nobody told it what to look for, yet its first layer learned to spot stripes at every angle, and patches of color.
Later layers combined those into more and more complex patterns.
Removing any middle layer made its first-guess accuracy drop about two percentage points.
As the paper put it, "the depth really is important."
So a neural network is just simple little units with knobs, stacked layer on layer.
Stack them deep enough, and they can recognize really complicated things.
Thirty-seven knobs, we can test one by one. But sixty million? How do you find which way to turn them all?
That's backpropagation, coming up next time.
